personality_voice.book_baseline: Hagrid in the books is warm, boisterous, emotionally transparent, fiercely loyal to Dumbledore, and prone to dramatic outbursts of anger (thundering at the Dursleys, leaping to his feet, threatening Vernon) followed by equally dramatic remorse ('Shouldn'ta lost me temper'). He is childlike in his enthusiasms - dragons, dangerous creatures, rock cakes no one can eat - and guileless to the point of self-sabotage, blurting out secrets he immediately regrets. His speech is phonetically rendered dialect, directly translated emotional states, and a pattern of escalating volume (from quiet worry to booming rage). He is also quietly perceptive: he changes subject when Snape comes up, he glances away when he is withholding something, and he shows genuine grief over Lily and James. His humor is incidental and warm rather than performed.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves almost all of this. Robbie Coltrane captures the boisterous entrance, the escalating anger at the Dursleys, the immediate remorse after giving Dudley a pig tail, the guileless secret-spilling ('I shouldn't have said that'), the weeping over Norbert, the childlike delight in the hatching dragon, and the warm loyalty to Dumbledore. The phonetic dialect is preserved. The pattern of emotional outbursts followed by embarrassed retreat is intact. The warmth toward Harry is consistent throughout.
personality_voice.difference: A handful of smaller texture moments are absent. The film omits Hagrid's detailed, unprompted opinions (his views on the Ministry of Magic, Cornelius Fudge, Slytherin history, Quidditch). His extended storytelling voice - the long narrations about Voldemort's rise, about Quirrell's backstory, about the Gringotts security - is compressed or cut. The scene where he carefully reassures Harry at Paddington ('Just be yerself') is absent, as is his quiet grief on Privet Drive ('Lily an' James dead'). The film shows him crying silently on Privet Drive but without the spoken lines. These are minor texture losses, not personality reversals.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main personality traits - warmth, loyalty, guilelessness, emotional volatility with quick remorse, childlike creature enthusiasm, dialect - are all directly evidenced in the film corpus. The losses are secondary: absence of the extended Voldemort backstory monologue (compressed into a shorter scene in the Leaky Cauldron), absence of the Ministry opinions, absence of the Paddington farewell scene. These reduce texture slightly but do not alter the character's dominant personality pattern. Minor penalty for simplification of secondary traits.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Hagrid serves multiple structural functions in Book 1: (1) the herald who delivers the call to adventure and explains the wizarding world to Harry; (2) the guide who physically escorts Harry through Diagon Alley and explains each institution; (3) the comic-yet-dangerous figure who accidentally leaks plot-critical information (Flamel, Fluffy's weakness, the Stone's location); (4) a grounding emotional figure who provides Harry with his first experience of genuine warmth and care; (5) an active agent who retrieves the Stone from Gringotts on Dumbledore's orders - a mission he completes successfully and mentions with pride. He initiates visits, writes notes, gives Harry birthday presents, invites him for tea, and in the forest sequence actively leads the investigation and protects the students with his crossbow.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves functions 1, 2, 3, and 4 largely intact. Hagrid as herald, guide, and leaky-secret-spiller are all directly evidenced. His forest role as protector and leader is maintained. The hospital scene at the end where he gives Harry the photo album is present and preserves the emotional grounding function.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several specific acts of agency are compressed or removed. The extended Diagon Alley guidance (Hagrid buying Harry an owl as a birthday present, advising on wands, explaining the Ministry, discussing Quidditch, defending Muggle-born wizards against Malfoy's implied slur) is partially cut - in the film Hagrid disappears before the wand scene ('I just got one more thing I got ter do') and is absent from several shop visits. The detailed tea scene where Hagrid notices the Gringotts article and deflects Harry's questions is removed - in the film this information is conveyed differently (Harry reads about it in a newspaper in the Great Hall and makes the connection himself without the tea scene context). The scene where Hagrid intervenes when Malfoy insults Ron's family by the Christmas tree ('He was provoked, Professor Snape') is absent. The Quidditch match scene where Hagrid watches from the stands and expresses worry about Harry's broom is preserved but compressed.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The primary structural role is preserved. Some secondary agency moments are cut (the tree corridor intervention, the extended shopping guidance). The most notable agency transfer: in the books, Hagrid's tea scene is where Harry first makes the Gringotts-Stone connection with Hagrid's visible evasion as the catalyst. In the film, Harry makes this connection himself in the Great Hall from a newspaper. This is a modest agency reduction - Hagrid's evasiveness is preserved in the later Philosopher's Stone conversation scene, but the specific moment of being the involuntary catalyst for Harry's deduction is redistributed. Overall role and agency are recognizable and largely intact.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Hagrid's motivations in Book 1 are: (1) fierce loyalty to Dumbledore, which makes him execute any task Dumbledore assigns without question; (2) love for Harry as the orphaned son of people he cared about - 'nicer people yeh couldn't find'; (3) a deep desire to be trusted and seen as capable and important ('He usually gets me ter do important stuff fer him. Fetchin' you - gettin' things from Gringotts - knows he can trust me, see'); (4) his lifelong love of dangerous creatures, which constitutes an internal conflict - he knows dragon-keeping is illegal and dangerous but cannot resist Norbert; (5) a loyalty conflict when he must keep secrets from Harry that puts him in visible distress (he doesn't meet Harry's eyes, changes subjects, blurts things and immediately retracts them). His remorse after revealing Fluffy's weakness is genuine and deep - he blames himself for potentially getting Harry killed.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: All five motivations are present in the film corpus. His pride in Dumbledore's trust is directly stated ('I'm on official Hogwarts business'). His love for Harry is shown through the birthday cake, the album, and the farewell. His creature obsession is fully intact through the Norbert arc. His loyalty conflict and guilt are shown in the hospital scene ('It's all my - ruddy - fault!') - though this specific scene is not in the provided film corpus, it is referenced indirectly; more precisely the film does show Hagrid's distress about revealing things he shouldn't. The internal conflict of knowing Norbert must go but being unable to let go is preserved.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film compresses the Leaky Cauldron scene where Hagrid narrates the Voldemort history, removing some of the emotional texture of how he relates to Lily and James's deaths personally ('knew yer mum an' dad, an' nicer people yeh couldn't find'). The motivation of personal grief intertwined with his care for Harry is present but less fully developed. His motivation of wanting to be seen as trustworthy and important is shown but not as explicitly stated ('He usually gets me ter do important stuff fer him') - the film cuts this self-aware pride monologue.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but still correct. The core drivers are all present and evidenced. The loss is in depth of articulation - the books let Hagrid voice his motivations more explicitly; the film shows them through action and compressed dialogue. No motivations are changed or replaced, only slightly less developed.

character_arc.book_baseline: Hagrid's arc in Book 1 is relatively flat in terms of fundamental personality change - he is the same warm, loyal, reckless figure at the end as at the beginning. However, he does undergo a meaningful emotional trajectory: starting as the confident herald who delivers Harry to his destiny, through the middle section where his recklessness (Norbert, leaking Fluffy's secret) creates problems, to the end where he experiences genuine guilt and remorse over his role in nearly getting Harry killed, and resolves this by giving Harry the photo album - an act of reparative love. The arc is less transformation than it is a cycle: confidence, recklessness, consequence, remorse, reparative gesture.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves this arc structurally. The confident herald opening is intact. The Norbert recklessness arc is intact. The guilt over Fluffy's secret is shown (hospital scene reference). The photo album gesture is the closing beat and is directly evidenced in the film corpus. The arc is compressed but the key points - opening confidence, mid-point recklessness with consequences, closing reparative gesture - are all present.
character_arc.difference: The film truncates the emotional beat of Hagrid in the hospital sobbing over his role in nearly getting Harry killed. In the book this scene is extended and explicit ('Yeh could've died! All fer a dragon egg! I'll never drink again! I should be chucked out an' made ter live as a Muggle!'). The film appears to condense or omit this specific moment based on the provided corpus. This is a meaningful compression because it is the emotional apex of the arc's consequence phase.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but structurally intact. The beginning, middle recklessness, and closing reparative gesture are all present. The specific hospital remorse scene is either cut or condensed, which removes the arc's most emotionally explicit moment, but the arc's logic remains legible from what remains. Minor penalty for compression of the emotional consequence beat.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Hagrid's two most important relationships in Book 1 are: (1) Hagrid-Harry: a quasi-parental warmth, the first adult who treats Harry as special and worthy rather than burdensome; Hagrid initiates contact, provides comfort, gives gifts, worries about Harry's wellbeing, and feels personally responsible for Harry's safety. (2) Hagrid-Dumbledore: absolute trust, devotion, and pride in being chosen by Dumbledore for important tasks; Hagrid is vocally defensive of Dumbledore's reputation and treats his trust as the highest possible honor. Secondary: Hagrid-Dursleys (contemptuous dismissal punctuated by threats) and Hagrid-Snape (defensive denial of Snape's guilt, a complex dynamic the books develop subtly through Hagrid's evasiveness).
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Hagrid-Harry relationship is well preserved: the birthday cake, the protective warmth through Diagon Alley, the farewell and photo album all demonstrate the quasi-parental dynamic. The Hagrid-Dumbledore devotion is explicitly stated ('I would trust Hagrid with my life'; Hagrid's defense of Dumbledore against Vernon). The Hagrid-Dursley dynamic is intact. The Hagrid-Snape dynamic is preserved in the denial scenes ('Codswallop. Professor Snape is a Hogwarts teacher').
key_relationships.difference: The Hagrid-Harry relationship loses some intimacy through compression - the Paddington farewell scene where Hagrid reassures Harry ('Don' you worry, Harry. You'll learn fast enough. Just be yerself') is absent from the film. Several smaller relationship-building moments across the year (the tea invitation note, the Christmas flute gift described in Harry's narration, the rock cake visits) are absent or glimpsed briefly. The emotional dynamic is correct but less developed.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The key relationships are mostly faithful in dynamic, tone, and function. The Hagrid-Harry quasi-parental warmth and the Hagrid-Dumbledore devotion are both clearly evidenced. Some compression of intimacy-building moments, but the emotional core of each relationship is preserved. Minor penalty for the loss of the Paddington scene which is the most explicit articulation of Hagrid's reassuring parental role.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The books give Hagrid several layers of complexity that prevent him from being merely a lovable giant: (1) He is unreliable as a keeper of secrets not through malice but through guilelessness and the inability to resist boasting about his importance - this is both endearing and genuinely creates danger for Harry; (2) He has a complicated relationship with his own status - expelled, wand snapped, technically not permitted to do magic, but allowed to stay on by Dumbledore's grace. He is visibly uncomfortable when Ollivander mentions his expelled status and grips the pink umbrella tightly. This is a source of insecurity that complicates his confident surface; (3) His opinions of institutional figures (Ministry = bunglers, Fudge = incompetent, Dumbledore = infallible) reveal a specific political naivety and uncritical loyalty that is not entirely admirable; (4) His creature obsession is presented not as charming eccentricity alone but as a genuine character flaw that puts others at risk and that he is unable to control even when he intellectually knows better; (5) The Norbert subplot explicitly shows his capacity for self-deception ('He's only a baby, after all'; packing Norbert a teddy bear while the dragon tears its head off); (6) He deflects Harry's questions about Snape with visible discomfort, suggesting he knows more than he says about Snape's history with Harry's parents - a nuance the film does not develop.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the secret-spilling guilelessness, the Norbert self-deception, and the Ollivander wand scene (though without the explicit discomfort about his expelled status - the film shows him gripping the umbrella but the line 'I've still got the pieces' and the exchange about whether he uses them is absent). The creature obsession as character flaw is intact. The Snape evasiveness is present but less textured.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The Ollivander scene loses the complexity around Hagrid's expelled status - in the books this is a moment where Hagrid's insecurity and shame are briefly visible ('Er -- yes, they did, yes,' shuffling his feet, then gripping the umbrella when asked if he uses it). The film cuts this exchange. The Ministry/Fudge opinions and political naivety are cut entirely. The Snape evasiveness exists but the specific scene where Hagrid 'didn't quite meet Harry's eyes' during the Snape conversation is harder to render in film and is not evidenced as preserved in the corpus. The extended Norbert aftermath - Hagrid becoming so consumed with Norbert that he neglects his gamekeeping duties, the brandy bottles and chicken feathers, the 'Mommy will never forget you' farewell - is compressed in the film but its emotional core (Hagrid calling Norbert 'Norbert' and performing maternal attachment) is present.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character retains substantial complexity: the guilelessness-as-flaw is intact, the creature obsession as self-destructive is intact, the Norbert self-deception is intact. The losses are real but secondary: the Ollivander shame moment, the Ministry/Fudge political naivety, the fuller Snape evasiveness texture. The film does not flatten Hagrid to a single trait; the complexity that remains is sufficient to understand the character as the books present him, though some nuance is lost.

lost_or_transferred_material: Hagrid's extended narration of Voldemort's rise at Privet Drive / hut (condensed into shorter Leaky Cauldron scene)
Paddington station farewell and Hagrid's reassurance ('Just be yerself')
Ollivander scene exchange about Hagrid's expelled status and broken wand ('I've still got the pieces'; grip of umbrella when asked if he uses it)
Hagrid's opinions on the Ministry of Magic and Cornelius Fudge as a bungler

Tea scene at Hagrid's hut where Harry discovers Gringotts newspaper article and Hagrid's visible evasion catalyzes Harry's deduction (Harry instead deduces this independently from newspaper in Great Hall in film)
Hagrid intervening for Ron when Malfoy insults his family by the Christmas tree corridor
Hagrid's gamekeeping neglect during Norbert period (brandy bottles, chicken feathers detail)
Hagrid's extended guilty breakdown in hospital wing after Stone crisis ('I'll never drink again! I should be chucked out an' made ter live as a Muggle!')
Hagrid's subtle evasiveness about Snape's history with Harry's parents (doesn't meet Harry's eyes)
Hagrid writing a note to Dumbledore via owl at the hut on the rock (small but characterizing moment of his loyal diligence)

Christmas flute gift (mentioned in book narration; absent in film's Christmas morning scene)
key_observations: The film adaptation of Hagrid in Philosopher's Stone is one of the more successful character translations in the series. The dominant personality traits - warm, boisterous, guileless, fiercely loyal, emotionally volatile, self-sabotaging through recklessness - are all directly evidenced in the film corpus, and Robbie Coltrane's performance captures the phonetic dialect and emotional transparency of the book character. The primary structural functions (herald, guide, comic-dangerous secret-spiller, emotional grounding figure) are preserved. The main losses are in textural depth: secondary scenes that add nuance (the Ollivander expelled-status discomfort, the Ministry political opinions, the Paddington farewell, the extended hospital guilt scene, the tea scene as catalyst for Harry's deduction) are compressed or cut. None of these individually constitute a fundamental misrepresentation of the character, but together they reduce the fullness of the book portrayal. The film Hagrid is recognizable, warm, and largely faithful - a slightly simplified but not distorted version of the book original.
